storm.summary_layperson: Periods of light rain continue through the evening, but this is a quiet, low-energy system with no thunderstorm risk — expect steady light rain rather than anything severe, in Riverside and the surrounding area alike.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer to speak of — Sound water (72.5°F) is actually running warmer than the air (64.4°F) already at 4 PM, an inverted gap that stays inverted through the evening, so the cove's usual protective mechanism isn't in play (moot anyway, since no storm cells are on radar).
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows no organized storm cells within range and no active NWS alerts. CAPE is essentially zero (20 J/kg), so today's rain is stratiform — a steady light-rain system moving through, not thunderstorm activity. The regional forecast calls for continued light rain this evening with a southeast gradient wind around 10 mph.

Normally the cove's move is to check whether the Sound's marine layer would blunt an approaching storm, but there's nothing to blunt today, and the mechanism itself isn't even set up: Sound water is at 72.5°F while the air is only 64.4°F — an inverted gap versus the usual summer pattern where cool water sits under warm air. No stable marine layer is present (marine layer strength: absent), and that inversion holds through the whole forecast window, not just right now.

Practical outcome: expect continued light rain through the 5–10 PM window with essentially no lightning or thunder risk, for Riverside and the surrounding towns alike. Nothing about the local geography changes the picture one way or the other tonight — there's no "Sound bubble" effect to lean on because there's no storm for it to work against.

What would change the call: a new NWS watch/advisory, a CAPE spike into the moderate range, or an actual convective cell appearing on KOKX. Absent any of those, treat tonight as a quiet, low-risk rain evening.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind, no sea breeze in play — expect it to keep easing through the window and wander in direction (SSE early, swinging to SW after sunset). Pressure favors the west side of the course, where Tod's Point isn't sheltering the flow. Start conservatively, don't commit hard to one persistent shift, and keep expectations modest — this is a light-air, finicky evening.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
DeltaT (inland air minus Sound water) is -8.1°F — well below the +5°F needed to drive a thermal sea breeze — and the pipeline's own sea-breeze proxy confirms it's inactive. This is a gradient-only day: whatever onshore flow exists is synoptic, riding along with tonight's rain system, not a thermal sea breeze. Current authoritative gradient (airport/open-water sites) averages 8.1 kt from the S–SSE, while RYC in the cove itself is reading lighter — SE 5.6 kt gusting 9, 10-min avg 4.4 kt.

That RYC/airport gap is exactly what the cove geography predicts for SE-ish flow: Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) partially shelters the east side of the course, so pressure favors the west side, where the flow isn't blocked.

The few HRRR hours available (5–7 PM) show the flow continuing to ease — down to 2.5–4.7 kt — while backing slightly further SSE, then swinging sharply to SW by 7 PM, right around sunset (6:54 PM). That's a genuine directional transition, not a tactical oscillation to play. Direction agreement across the full station network is only 0.57 (below the 0.7 coherence threshold), consistent with a light, unsettled wind field rather than a clean, steady gradient flow.

Data gap: HRRR forecast data cuts off after 7 PM (f05–f12 fetch failures), so the 8–10 PM rows in the table are extrapolated from the late trend (light, SW-ish) rather than pulled from the model — treat the second half of the window with low confidence.

Bottom line: a light, easing breeze all evening with no sea breeze to lean on, swinging from SSE to SW after sunset. Favor the west side of the course, don't commit hard to a shift, and expect drifter-to-light-air conditions (3–6 kt) for most of the window.
